name: Routing Across Automated Market Makers
title: Routing Across Automated Market Makers
answer: Routing across automated market makers is the practice of choosing and sequencing trades across multiple liquidity pools rather than sending an order to a single pool. It covers multi-hop paths, order splitting, and the comparison of quotes from different AMM protocols. The scope includes both simple swaps and more complex routes that pass through several tokens or chains. It also includes the routers, aggregators, and solver systems that compute those paths. The field sits inside crypto markets and decentralised finance, where execution quality is measured by output amount, price impact, and cost.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Routing across automated market makers is the practice of choosing and sequencing trades across multiple liquidity pools rather than sending an order to a single pool. It covers multi-hop paths, order splitting, and the comparison of quotes from different AMM protocols. The scope includes both simple swaps and more complex routes that pass through several tokens or chains. It also includes the routers, aggregators, and solver systems that compute those paths. The field sits inside crypto markets and decentralised finance, where execution quality is measured by output amount, price impact, and cost.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: Routing runs on public blockchains and the smart contracts that hold AMM pools, with execution settled on chain. Off-chain components include nodes, RPC providers, indexers, and price or liquidity APIs that feed route calculations. Many routers also rely on mempools, relayers, and solver networks to submit transactions or bundles. Gas costs, block times, and layer two environments shape what routes are practical. Well-known AMMs such as Uniswap, Curve, and Balancer are common venues, though any pool with a compatible interface can be included.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The work starts by gathering pool states and quotes, then modelling each possible path as a graph of tokens and pools. A router or solver searches that graph for routes that maximise output after fees, gas, and expected slippage. Orders may be split across several pools or executed in sequence to reduce price impact. Simulation and historical data help estimate outcomes before a transaction is signed. On chain, the chosen route is executed atomically, so either all steps succeed or the whole transaction reverts.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk in routing centre on smart contract exposure, transaction ordering, and the provenance of quotes. A route can fail because of slippage, liquidity changes, or a revert, and users may pay gas even when no swap occurs. MEV, frontrunning, and sandwich attacks can worsen execution, while opaque solver behaviour makes it hard to know why a route was chosen. Audits, open source code, and on-chain records provide some provenance, but they do not remove counterparty or protocol risk. Regulatory treatment of AMMs and aggregators varies by jurisdiction and continues to develop.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Routing is moving toward intent based systems, where a user states a desired outcome and solvers compete to find an execution path. Cross chain routing and account abstraction are expanding the set of venues and the ways transactions can be paid for. Batch auctions and private order flow are being explored to reduce MEV and improve fairness. Machine learning is increasingly used to predict liquidity, gas, and slippage, though the final execution remains on chain. The direction is toward more automated, multi venue execution with greater transparency about how routes are selected.
